title: Santa Barbara Corpus of Spoken American English, parts 1–4
authors_year: Du Bois et al.; UCSB corpus
inspected: UCSB corpus overview, access and contents/summaries sections (HTML downloaded).
finding: The site offers free TRN transcripts and CHAT versions, audio and timestamps aligned at the intonation-unit level; it describes parts 1–4 as approximately 249,000 words.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Treat natural speech as timed, multi-unit interaction, not alternating polished one-liners.
limitations: The entire corpus includes noncasual genres; the quantitative entries below use a selected four-file sample.

title: SBCSAE SBC002: Lambada
authors_year: Du Bois et al.; UCSB corpus
inspected: Full SBC002.trn downloaded and parsed with sbcsae/measure.py. Group conversation about dance and a movie. Speaker turns are contiguous timestamped units with same assigned speaker; counts exclude zero-word turns. Text only, no audio listening.
finding: 645 lexical turns: median 5 words; 48.8% <=4 words, 13.0% >=15 words. 1258 lexical intonation units: median 3.0 words (mean 4.02). Filler tokens/phrases uh 15, um 4, like 73, I mean 33, you know 23; 154 laughter-marked units, 616 overlap-opening marks, 173 cut-off marks.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Let one character sustain a thought across several short intonation units and another answer briefly; vary long and short turns.
limitations: Exploratory four-file convenience sample, not representative of all US talk. Continuation rows inherit most recent named speaker (can misassign amid overlap); fillers are literal matches, like includes lexical uses; bracket openings are notation marks, not interruptions; @/Hx indicates laughter-marked unit, not laughs; hyphens and double dashes are mechanical cut-off proxies.

title: Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation
inspected: Full PNAS article PDF downloaded and text extracted; examined methods and response-time distribution/results.
finding: Across 10 languages, measured responses to questions in informal conversations cluster around very short gaps; the highest frequency of transitions falls between 0 and 200 ms, although average offsets differ culturally.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Let the reply often begin almost at completion, with occasional overlap or a meaningful delay rather than a mechanical pause every time.
limitations: Measured question–answer transitions, not every turn; PDF font extraction mangles some minus signs and symbols, so no inferred median is quoted.

title: Timing in turn-taking and its implications for processing models of language
inspected: Full Frontiers HTML article downloaded and read, especially abstract and timing/planning discussion.
finding: The article describes average interturn gaps around 200 ms, versus speech-production latencies above 600 ms; prospective responders therefore begin planning while they are still listening.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Write replies that latch onto a projected ending, including mistaken anticipation and late course correction.
limitations: Timing generalization is across analyzed conversational datasets, not a prescription for every emotionally loaded pause.

title: The preference for self-correction in the organization of repair in conversation
inspected: Cambridge article landing page and abstract downloaded; full paper was access-gated.
finding: The abstract identifies a conversational organization addressing trouble in speaking, hearing and understanding, with a strong empirical skew toward self-repair rather than correction by others.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Let a speaker fix their own phrasing before a listener supplies the polished version.
limitations: Abstract only; no claim about exact repair rates or detailed sequential mechanisms.

title: Universal principles in the repair of communication problems
inspected: Full PLOS HTML article downloaded; read abstract and frequency/types sections.
finding: Other-initiated repair appears on average about once per 1.4 minutes in the languages sampled; speakers use open, restricted and candidate-understanding requests and favor the most specific usable one.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: When something is missed, use a targeted check (the name? this Friday?) rather than a universal Huh? every time.
limitations: Cross-linguistic conversation sample; 1.4 minutes is an aggregate, not an individual-scene quota.

title: Using uh and um in spontaneous speaking
inspected: Full Cognition article PDF downloaded and text extracted; read abstract, proposal and reported contrast in following delays.
finding: Their proposal treats uh as announcing a relatively minor expected delay and um a more substantial one; their data show sharper differences in following than preceding delays.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Put a filler where a character is holding the floor while searching or deciding, not evenly across sentences.
limitations: Interpretation of fillers is a proposed account, not an invariant meaning; PDF text extraction contains minor font/ligature artifacts.

title: Basic meanings of you know and I mean
inspected: Full Journal of Pragmatics article PDF downloaded and text extracted; read abstract and opening discussion.
finding: The article analyzes you know as inviting listener inference and I mean as warning of a coming adjustment; these phrases are not interchangeable filler.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Use you know to enlist shared understanding, and I mean when a speaker revises or qualifies what was just said.
limitations: The basic-meaning analysis is the authors’ synthesis; individual tokens can have context-sensitive functions.

title: Laughter
inspected: Full American Scientist article HTML downloaded; read field-observation, punctuation-effect and speaker-versus-audience passages.
finding: In the reported field observations, fewer than 20% of sampled laughs responded to structured jokes or stories; speakers laughed about 46% more often than audiences, and laughter tended to punctuate speech rather than interrupt it mid-phrase.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Let the speaker laugh at their own ordinary remark and allow the listener to respond without a laugh.
limitations: This is a 1996 popular-science account of fieldwork, not a directly analyzed full 1993 journal article; observation context and definitions matter.

title: Jocular mockery, (dis)affiliation and face
inspected: Griffith repository record and full abstract downloaded; manuscript listed but not opened.
finding: The abstract treats jocular mockery as an interactional move whose responses can align or disalign with earlier action and index affiliation or disaffiliation as relationships evolve.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: After a tease, write the target’s reaction as consequential: play along, resist, or answer seriously; do not guarantee a joke in return.
limitations: Abstract only; no transcript examples or quantified frequency of reactions inspected.

title: Overlapping talk and the organization of turn-taking for conversation
inspected: Cambridge article landing page and abstract downloaded; full PDF not inspected.
finding: The abstract distinguishes overlapping talk as an interactional phenomenon participants sometimes treat as problematic and resolve through organized practices; simultaneous speech is not automatically equivalent to hostile interruption.
label: Evidence
writer_takeaway: Make overlapping talk context-dependent, and show whether participants yield, persist, or repair the collision.
limitations: Abstract only; no numerical overlap rate or detailed examples inspected.
